Helping Children and Young People Navigate Grief, Loss and Change

Grief can be difficult for children and adolescents to understand and express.

When someone important dies, a family changes, a relationship ends, or a child experiences a significant change in their life, they may not always have the words to explain what they are feeling.

Grief can look different from one child to another.

Some children may talk openly about their feelings. Others may become quieter, more emotional, frustrated, withdrawn or worried. Some may appear to cope well initially and experience stronger feelings later.

There is no single "right" way for a child to grieve.

Therapy can provide a safe, age-appropriate space for children and young people to understand their feelings, adjust to change and receive support as they navigate their loss.

What Is Grief and Loss?

Grief is a natural response to losing someone, something or a way of life that is important to us.

For children and young people, loss can include:

  • The death of a parent, sibling, family member, friend or another important person
  • The death of a pet
  • Separation from someone they are close to
  • Parents separating or significant family changes
  • Moving away from family, friends or a familiar community
  • Serious illness or injury affecting themselves or someone they love
  • Missing school or activities because of illness
  • Changes in independence or physical abilities
  • Losing opportunities to participate in activities they enjoy
  • Other significant changes that alter their sense of safety, connection or everyday life

Children's Health Queensland highlights that children experiencing serious illness or injury may experience grief through changes such as time away from friends, missing school, reduced mobility, reduced independence and missing activities they enjoy.

Grief Doesn't Always Look Like Sadness

Children may not always express grief in the way adults expect.

You might notice:

  • Sadness or tearfulness
  • Irritability or anger
  • Increased emotional reactions
  • Withdrawal from family or friends
  • Changes in sleep
  • Changes in appetite
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Reduced interest in activities
  • Worry or anxiety
  • Becoming more dependent on parents or carers
  • Wanting to talk about the person or situation repeatedly
  • Asking questions about what happened
  • Appearing to return to their usual activities and then becoming upset again

Some children may also communicate their feelings through play, drawing, creative activities or changes in behaviour rather than through direct conversation.

There is no single pattern that defines grief.

Children's Health Queensland emphasises that there is no right or wrong way to grieve, and that people respond to loss differently.

When a Child Is Grieving

Children may move in and out of grief rather than experiencing it as a continuous feeling.

They may be deeply upset one moment and then want to play, laugh or talk about something completely different.

This does not necessarily mean they have stopped grieving.

Children may need opportunities to:

  • Ask questions
  • Express feelings in their own way
  • Talk about the person or experience
  • Maintain important routines
  • Spend time with supportive people
  • Return to enjoyable activities
  • Understand changes in their family or environment
  • Feel safe asking difficult questions

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

You may be considering therapy because your child or teenager:

  • Has experienced the death of someone important
  • Is struggling after a significant family change
  • Is finding it difficult to adjust after a separation or move
  • Has experienced illness or injury
  • Seems unusually sad, angry or withdrawn
  • Is having difficulty returning to everyday activities
  • Is struggling at school following a loss
  • Has become anxious or worried about further loss
  • Is finding friendships or family relationships more difficult
  • Continues to struggle with the loss and you are unsure how to help
  • Wants to talk about their experience but does not know how
  • Has difficulty expressing what they are feeling

You may also be seeking support because you are unsure whether what your child is experiencing is part of grief or whether they need additional professional support.

You don't need to know the answer before reaching out.

How Can Parents Support a Grieving Child?

Create a Safe Space

Let your child know that it is okay to talk about what has happened and that they can express their feelings in ways that feel comfortable for them.

This might involve talking, drawing, writing, playing or spending time together.

Children's Health Queensland recommends creating a safe space where children can express their feelings in a way that feels comfortable for them.

Be Honest and Age Appropriate

Children often have questions about what has happened.

Use simple, clear and honest language that is appropriate for their developmental level. Allow your child to ask questions and give them opportunities to return to the conversation as they need to.

Children's Health Queensland specifically recommends direct, age-appropriate communication and avoiding euphemisms when talking with children about difficult experiences.

Maintain Familiar Routines

Where possible, maintaining familiar routines can give children a sense of comfort and predictability during a period of change.

School, meals, bedtime, activities and time with supportive people can provide important structure.

Allow Their Grief to Be Different From Yours

Parents and children may respond to the same loss differently.

One child may want to talk frequently, while another may prefer quiet time. One family member may express their emotions openly, while another may focus on practical tasks.

Different responses do not mean that one person is grieving "better" than another.

Keep Connection Available

Your child may not always want to talk.

Let them know that you are available when they are ready.

A simple message such as:

"You don't have to talk about it right now. I'm here whenever you want to."

can help keep communication open.

How Can Therapy Help?

Grief therapy for children and adolescents is not about making grief disappear.

It can provide a safe space where a young person can understand and express what they are experiencing while gradually adjusting to life after a significant loss or change. Depending on the child's age and individual circumstances, therapy may support:

  • Understanding and expressing emotions
  • Making sense of what has happened
  • Processing difficult feelings
  • Developing healthy coping strategies
  • Managing anxiety or worry
  • Adjusting to changes in family or everyday life
  • Rebuilding confidence and a sense of safety
  • Maintaining meaningful connections and memories
  • Returning to school and everyday activities
  • Strengthening communication with parents or carers
  • Developing age-appropriate ways of remembering and expressing loss

The approach will depend on the child's developmental stage, circumstances, relationship to the loss and individual needs.

Supporting Children After the Death of Someone Important

When a child loses someone they love, there may be changes throughout the family.

Children may notice changes in routines, family roles, relationships and everyday life.

They may also continue to have questions or feelings about the person over time.

There is no fixed point at which grief is expected to be "finished."

Children's Health Queensland describes grief as something that can require families to adjust and readjust over time, particularly following significant loss.

For some families, talking about the person who has died, remembering them and continuing to acknowledge their importance can be a meaningful part of adapting to the loss.

What Could Change With the Right Support?

With appropriate support, a child or teenager may gradually:

  • Feel more comfortable expressing emotions
  • Understand their grief more clearly
  • Develop ways of coping with difficult moments
  • Feel less alone in their experience
  • Adjust to changes in everyday life
  • Re-engage with school, friendships and activities
  • Communicate more openly with trusted adults
  • Develop a stronger sense of safety and stability
  • Find age-appropriate ways to remember and maintain meaningful connections

The goal is not to "move on" or forget the person, relationship or experience.

It is about helping the young person learn to live with the changes while continuing to grow and participate in life.

When Should You Seek Professional Support?

Grief itself is not something that needs to be treated simply because a child is grieving.

However, additional support may be helpful when a child or adolescent is struggling to adjust or when their emotional wellbeing and everyday functioning are significantly affected.

Consider seeking professional support if your child:

  • Is finding it increasingly difficult to participate in everyday activities
  • Is persistently withdrawn from family or friends
  • Is struggling significantly at school
  • Is experiencing ongoing anxiety or emotional distress
  • Is having difficulty communicating about what they are experiencing
  • Is finding family relationships increasingly difficult
  • Appears unable to adjust to significant changes in their life
  • You are concerned about how they are coping and do not know what to do next

You do not have to wait until you are certain that therapy is necessary.

A conversation with an appropriate professional can help you understand what support may be suitable.

Supporting the Whole Family

When a child experiences a significant loss, parents and carers may be grieving too.

This can make it particularly difficult to know how to support your child while managing your own emotions.

Children's Health Queensland recognises that parents and carers can experience multiple layers of loss and that grief can affect the wider family and community.

Seeking support for yourself can also be an important part of supporting your child.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

It can be difficult to know whether your child needs grief counselling, psychological therapy, family support or simply some additional guidance around how to support them at home.

You don't need to diagnose the problem before contacting us.

At MBP, our role is to help you understand your options and connect you with an appropriate practitioner based on your child's or teenager's age, circumstances, presenting concerns and available services.

We can help make the first steps clearer.

Why Families Choose MBP

When your family is already navigating a significant loss or change, finding the right support can feel overwhelming.

MBP can help by:

  • Listening to your concerns
  • Understanding your child's circumstances
  • Helping identify appropriate practitioner options
  • Considering your child's age and presenting needs
  • Helping you understand the referral and intake process
  • Supporting the administrative steps involved in getting started

You don't have to figure everything out before reaching out.

Start With a Conversation

If your child or teenager is finding it difficult to cope with a significant loss or change, professional support may provide a safe space for them to talk, process their experience and develop ways to move forward.

You don't need to know exactly what your child needs before you contact us.
